Notes after the Brackley warehouse review

I spent most of last week at the Brackley site, and I want to set down what I saw before the details fade. The brief was simple on paper; the reality was not. The client wanted to know why their picking rate had fallen by a fifth over two quarters, and they wanted an answer they could act on before the autumn peak. What follows is my attempt to analyse what is going on, and to say plainly what I think they should do next.

The first thing to say is that nobody on the floor is lazy. That matters, because the management summary I was handed reads as though the problem were one of effort. It is not. In practice the pickers are working harder than they were a year ago; they are walking further, waiting longer at the packing benches, and spending a good deal of their shift hunting for stock that the system says is in one place and is actually in another. The upshot is that effort has gone up and output has gone down, which is precisely the pattern you would expect from a layout problem rather than a people problem.

There is a certain zeitgeist in warehouse management at the moment, and Brackley has caught it badly. The zeitgeist says that every problem can be solved with more data, more dashboards and more scanning. I have nothing against data; I spend my working life trying to analyse it properly. But the zeitgeist tends to skip the part where somebody walks the floor with a notebook and asks the people doing the work what slows them down. At Brackley nobody had done that for well over a year, and the dashboards had quietly drifted away from what was happening in the aisles. If I could retire one word from the industry for a season, zeitgeist would be near the top of the list, if only because the thing it describes has done so much damage.

Let me describe the layout. The fast-moving lines, the ones that account for most of the daily picks, are stored at the far end of the building, towards the goods-in doors. This made sense three years ago, when the site handled mostly bulk replenishment and the fast lines were the ones arriving in volume. It makes no sense now. The business has shifted towards small, frequent orders, and the pickers spend a large share of every route walking past slow stock to reach the lines they need. Whilst I was there I followed four pickers through a full wave each, and the pattern was the same every time: a long walk out, a cluster of picks, a long walk back.

There was a minor kerfuffle on the second morning when I asked to see the slotting rules. Nobody could find them. Eventually a shift lead produced a printed sheet from a drawer; it was dated, it was annotated in three different hands, and it contradicted the system in several places. I mention the kerfuffle not to embarrass anyone but because it tells you something important. The rules that decide where stock lives had stopped being anybody's job. When a rule is nobody's job, it decays; when it decays, the floor compensates; and when the floor compensates, the numbers start to lie.

In practice, what the floor had done was build a second, informal layout on top of the official one. Experienced pickers knew that a certain line was really kept on the end of an aisle, not in its assigned bay, because that was where the replenishment team found room for it. New starters did not know this, and they walked to the assigned bay, found it empty, and either raised a query or went looking. The upshot is that the site depends on memory, and memory leaves when people do. Turnover at Brackley has been high this year; I do not think that is a coincidence.

Now to the packing benches. There are six of them, arranged in a row along the eastern wall, and four were staffed on each shift I observed. The queue at the benches built up every afternoon; pickers waited, sometimes for several minutes, with full trolleys. Whilst they waited, they were not picking. The managers I spoke to had noticed the queue but treated it as a separate problem, owned by a separate team, with a separate budget. I would gently suggest that it is the same problem seen from the other end. If you speed up picking without fixing packing, you simply move the queue.

So what should they do? I would make three changes, in this order.

First, re-slot the fast lines. Move the top movers to the bays nearest the packing benches, and move the slow stock out towards the goods-in end. This is not glamorous work; it takes a weekend, a careful plan and a lot of pallet trucks. But in practice it is the change that buys the most time back for the least money, and it can be done before the peak. I would analyse the order history for the last ninety days to decide what counts as fast, rather than relying on the annual figures, which are badly skewed by last winter.

Second, give the slotting rules an owner. One named person, with the authority to change the rules and the duty to keep the system and the floor in step. That person should walk the aisles every week; they should have a short list of exceptions to clear; and they should be the one who decides when a line moves. You can't eat your cake and have it too: either the system is the truth, or the floor's memory is the truth, and at the moment Brackley is trying to have both and getting the worst of each.

Third, staff the benches to the afternoon peak rather than to the daily average. This is a rota question, not a capital one. The upshot of averaging is that you are overstaffed in the morning and understaffed when it matters; the queue I saw every afternoon is the direct result.

I should say what I would not do. I would not buy new software this year. The current system is perfectly capable; the problem is that what it is told no longer matches what is on the shelves. Nor would I bring in incentive pay for pick rates, which several people suggested to me. Incentives built on a broken layout reward the people who know the informal map and punish the people who follow the official one. That is the opposite of what the site needs.

There is a broader point here, and it is one I keep returning to. Most of the problems I am asked to analyse are not caused by any single bad decision. They are caused by good decisions that were right once and were never revisited. Storing the fast lines at the far end was a good decision; so was letting experienced pickers work around gaps; so was splitting packing into its own team. Each made sense on the day it was made. Taken together, years later, they produce a site that works hard and moves slowly.

I will write up the slotting plan in more detail next week, with a list of the lines I would move first and a rough schedule for the weekend. I would welcome comments, particularly from the shift leads, who know the floor far better than I do. The aim is to have the new layout in place and settled well before the peak, so that the site goes into the busy season with the walking cut down and the queue at the benches gone.

One last note, which is more of a reminder to myself than advice to the client. When I arrived I had a theory, and it was wrong; I thought the problem would turn out to be the scanners, which are old and occasionally slow. The scanners are fine. I only found that out by watching people work, which is a lesson I seem to need to learn again on every job.
